title: How we hacked YC Spring 2025 batch’s AI agents — Rene Brandel, Casco

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is security vulnerabilities in AI agent systems, covering IDOR, arbitrary code execution, SSRF, credential theft, and authorization failures. The talk is about red-teaming AI agents for security vulnerabilities, fitting security_defense; the issues are cross-domain web security principles applied broadly. The talk covers testing (red-teaming agents), deployment (production vulnerabilities), and design (recommendations for secure agent architecture). Assumes familiarity with web security concepts and agent architectures, but explains vulnerabilities accessibly with concrete examples. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All claims are directly stated in the transcript with specific character-anchored excerpts.

summary: Rene Brandel introduces himself as CEO of Casco, a YC company focused on red teaming AI agents. He contrasts early complex multi-cloud agent architectures with today's normalized stacks comprising server, frontend, API server, LLM, tools, and data sources. While this normalization is beneficial, Brandel argues security discussions have been too narrowly focused on LLM-specific issues like prompt injection, when real damage occurs across the entire system. To make a splashy internal YC launch, Casco set 30-minute timers and hacked 7 of 16 publicly-accessible YC X25 agents. The first common vulnerability is Cross-User Data Access via IDOR: agents had tools to look up users, documents, and chats by ID without authorization checks. Attackers extracted user IDs from demo videos and traversed interconnected IDs. The fix requires both authentication and authorization, using access control matrices like Supabase row-level security. Agents should be treated as users, not API servers. The second vulnerability is Arbitrary Code Execution via code sandboxes. One hacked agent had a code sandbox with read/write Python file permissions. Attackers explored the filesystem, found app.py with security protections, overwrote it with empty strings to bypass checks, then used service endpoint discovery to steal service tokens, ultimately accessing all customer data via BigQuery. Brandel strongly advises against rolling custom code sandboxes, recommending out-of-the-box solutions like ETB that use Firecracker for proper isolation, noting that containers alone are not an isolation layer. The third vulnerability is Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): attackers extracted a system prompt revealing a tool that pulled database schema from a private GitHub repo. By coercing the agent to use a malicious git URL (badacctor.com test.git), they captured the agent's GitHub credentials and downloaded the entire private codebase. Key takeaways are: agent security is bigger than just LLM security, treat agents as users, and don't roll your own code sandbox. In Q&A, Brandel mentions hidden layer.com's policy puppeteering attack blog post for system prompt extraction techniques and contrasts local yolo mode with server-side sandbox isolation. Casco offers an AI agent that actively attacks other AI agents to identify security vulnerabilities at casco.com.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agent security must encompass the entire system, not just LLM-specific threats like prompt injection
Agents should be treated as users, not API servers—they should not have service-level permissions or determine authorization patterns
IDOR vulnerabilities allow attackers to traverse interconnected IDs and access other users' data when only authentication is checked without authorization
Code execution sandboxes with seemingly innocent read/write file permissions can be exploited to bypass security checks and steal service tokens
Don't roll your own code sandboxes—use out-of-the-box solutions with proper isolation like Firecracker, not mere containers
SSRF vulnerabilities allow attackers to coerce agents into calling unintended endpoints, leaking credentials to attacker-controlled servers
Always sanitize inputs and outputs, applying traditional web application security principles to agent architectures
Service tokens are rarely configured with granular least-privilege permissions, making stolen tokens highly dangerous
Identify IDOR vulnerabilities in agent tool definitions that allow cross-user data access
Understand why agents should be treated as users with user-level permissions rather than services with service-level permissions

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Rene Brandel introduces himself as CEO of Casco, a YC company specializing in red teaming AI agents. He shares his background at AWS and a voice-to-code hackathon project from 10 years ago, contrasting early complex multi-cloud agent architectures with today's normalized stacks.

sections.title: Why Casco Hacked AI Agents
sections.summary: Casco wanted a splashy YC internal launch and set 30-minute timers to hack publicly-accessible YC X25 agents. They hacked 7 of 16 agents and earned the second-highest upvoted launch post in YC history. The approach involved leaking system prompts, examining tool definitions, and attempting exploits.

sections.title: Common Issue 1: Cross-User Data Access (IDOR)
sections.summary: The first common vulnerability is IDOR. Agents had tools to look up users, documents, and chats by ID without authorization checks. Attackers extracted user IDs from demo videos and traversed interconnected IDs across the system. The fix requires both authentication and authorization, using access control matrices like Supabase row-level security. Agents should be treated as users, not services.

sections.title: Common Issue 2: Arbitrary Code Execution
sections.summary: The second vulnerability involves code execution sandboxes. One hacked agent had a code sandbox with read/write Python file permissions. Attackers explored the filesystem, found app.py with security protections, overwrote it with empty strings to bypass checks, then used service endpoint discovery to steal service tokens and access all customer data via BigQuery. Brandel strongly advises against rolling custom code sandboxes, recommending out-of-the-box solutions like ETB with proper isolation and MCP server integration.

sections.title: Common Issue 3: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
sections.summary: The third vulnerability is SSRF. An extracted system prompt revealed a tool that pulled database schema from a private GitHub repository. Attackers coerced the agent into using a malicious git URL (badacctor.com test.git), causing the agent to send GitHub credentials to an attacker-controlled server. With those credentials, they downloaded the entire private codebase. Brandel emphasizes thinking through system implications and always sanitizing inputs and outputs.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Brandel presents three main takeaways: agent security is bigger than just LLM security, treat agents as users (applies to authentication and input sanitization), and don't roll your own code sandbox. These are the most basic issues observed, with many more security concerns existing beyond them.

sections.title: Casco's Solution and Contact Information
sections.summary: Casco built an AI agent that actively attacks other AI agents to identify where they break. Brandel invites attendees to book a demo at casco.com and connect on LinkedIn or Twitter.

sections.title: Q&A
sections.summary: Brandel recommends hidden layer.com's blog post on policy puppeteering attacks for system prompt extraction techniques. On sandbox security, he contrasts local yolo mode (like Cursor) with server-side sandboxes, noting sandboxes typically use Firecracker under the hood for proper isolation. He cautions that containers alone are not an isolation layer.

demonstrations: Extracting a user ID from a product demo video URL and using it to access another user's personal information via IDOR
Traversing interconnected IDs (user ID, chat ID, document ID) to move through an entire system
Using a code sandbox's read permission to explore the filesystem and discover app.py with security protections
Overwriting app.py with empty strings to bypass all security checks in a code sandbox
Using service endpoint discovery to fetch service tokens and scopes from within a container
Querying BigQuery with a stolen service token to access all customer data
Substituting a malicious git URL (badacctor.com test.git) in an agent tool to capture GitHub credentials via SSRF
Downloading an entire private codebase using stolen git credentials obtained through SSRF
limitations: Only 16 publicly-accessible YC X25 agents were tested, so findings may not generalize to all agent deployments
Each agent was given only a 30-minute time limit for hacking, potentially missing deeper vulnerabilities
